layers.title: Borders
layers.status: reconstruction
layers.legend: Borders: Cliopatria v0.2.1 (Bennett et al. 2025), CC BY 4.0 – processed by Vitruvian Manager
layers.method: The borders are Cliopatria’s, release v0.2.1 (Ed Chalstrey and James Bennett, Seshat Global History Databank, Zenodo, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23128623), described in J. S. Bennett et al., 'Cliopatria - A geospatial database of world-wide political entities from 3400BCE to 2024CE', Scientific Data 12, 247 (2025), https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-025-04516-9. Licence: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). What Cliopatria says of its coverage: its README calls it a dataset of worldwide polities from 3400 BCE to 2024 CE, with over 1,600 political entities sampled at varying timesteps and spatial scales. Release v0.2.1 holds 13,797 rows, and fewer than 20 in any century before 800 BC, so the map shows few polities in those years. How Cliopatria draws them, from its paper: a polity is drawn where one or more written sources attest to it and indicate its location and extent in particular years, so a polity that no written source attests, such as the Xia Dynasty before 1600 BC in the paper’s example, is not drawn; with rare exceptions a polity occupies at least 5,000 km² and lasts at least 50 years. Its README says the maps reflect only one version of the territory held by past polities, that border uncertainties and differing opinions on the names, territorial changes and durations of polities are common challenges for historians, and that users of the data are responsible for judging whether it suits their purpose; the paper says the dataset does not encode border uncertainty or territorial disputes. These are a research dataset’s borders, made to compare polities across the world and five thousand years: they are coarser than a survey’s, and no line on the map is a surveyed boundary. Its rows carry no field naming which atlas or regional source each outline came from (the paper lists its sources by region). Each row holds from its first year to its last, both included. Cliopatria writes years before AD 1 as negative numbers; VM reads -1 as 1 BC, with no year 0, so the six rows that end at year 0 are drawn to 1 BC. RELATION rows (vassalages, alliances, unions) are drawn as outlines over the polities they join. A name in parentheses, such as "(Kingdom of France)", is a composite polity, an entity together with its dependencies: Cliopatria’s paper says composite polities "are denoted in the database by enclosing their name in parentheses". VM draws a composite polity as a dashed outline, like a RELATION row, so its core is not filled twice; in a download each row keeps its own area, so a composite’s area and its parts' areas must not be added together. Changes by Vitruvian Manager: every row, 3400 BC to AD 2024, in 17 files by years (a row spanning two files is in both; the page loads a file only when the frame reaches its years), converted to TopoJSON with topojson-server 3.0.1, coordinates quantised to 1/100,000 of each file’s extent (points that then coincide are merged; no simplification), with a row id added (cl- and ten hex digits of the sha256 of the row’s name, years and type). Precision: VM counts a border before 1500 as known only to its century (VM’s rule for Cliopatria before AD 1500, set out with the click’s rules in omni/README.md, "How a click sets the view"); from 1500 the years are Cliopatria’s, which VM has not checked. A Q-id is drawn only where Wikidata’s names for Cliopatria’s id agree with the row’s name and Wikidata’s years for it meet the row’s own years, or where a Master Index place of that name and those years matches; elsewhere VM says it cannot outline the entity. VM holds borders for 3400 BC–AD 2024, the years Cliopatria covers.

layers.title: Battles
layers.status: as Wikidata records them
layers.legend: Battles: Wikidata (CC0), each date and point with its Wikidata item and property
layers.method: VM’s own text. The 1,966 battles VM holds with a date and a point, 1258 to 2025: every conflict of the Master Index that Wikidata types a battle (P31 Q178561), and every located battle of War Focus, each read from Wikidata by omni/scripts/build-battles.mjs: its point in time (P585), or its start and end (P580, P582), at the precision and in the calendar Wikidata records, never converted; its coordinate location (P625) as Wikidata gives it, with its precision; and what supports each value, by VM’s rule: a reference naming a work (P248), a reference URL or a database record counts as a reference; a value only imported from a Wikipedia (P143, P4656) reads ‘Wikipedia-sourced, unverified’; anything less reads ‘no reference’. A battle with no date or no point in Wikidata is left out, and so is one whose year no battle can have (before 3000 BC). 1,912 are tied to a war of VM’s war registry (omni/data/layers/wars/registry.json), 1,912 of them to a war War Focus covers, which a click opens. Above 2,000 drawn at once, the points cluster. Wikidata’s data is CC0. Each view says how many battles VM holds for its years.

layers.method: VM’s own text. Today’s countries, from Natural Earth’s Admin 0 – Countries at 1:110 million, release v5.1.1 (13 May 2022), with a point for each of the 64 small states and territories that file leaves out (the Siachen Glacier, which Natural Earth calls indeterminate, is not one), at the label point Natural Earth’s 1:50 million file gives it. Natural Earth is in the public domain. Its borders are de facto ones, as Natural Earth draws them, and they are today’s: the design keeps today’s map off every year before 1886, so VM draws this base only from 1886, and a by-country value of a year before 2022 is drawn on today’s borders, which the legend says. Each country is joined to by-country data by its ISO 3166 alpha-3 code: Natural Earth’s ISO_A3, else its ISO_A3_EH, else XKX for Kosovo, the code the World Bank uses; N. Cyprus and Somaliland have no code and take no value. Each country also keeps the Wikidata id Natural Earth gives it (WIKIDATAID), for joins by Q-id. Converted to TopoJSON by topojson-server 3.0.1, quantised to 1/100,000 of the world’s extent, with no simplification (omni/scripts/build-countries.mjs).

layers.space: by country, drawn on today’s borders (Natural Earth v5.1.1, 2022)

layers.status: as the World Bank estimates it

style.unit: people per km² of land area

layers.legend: Population density: World Bank, World Development Indicators, EN.POP.DNST (CC BY 4.0), on Natural Earth’s countries of today
layers.method: VM’s own text, quoting the World Bank. The World Bank’s Population density (people per sq. km of land area) (EN.POP.DNST), from its World Development Indicators, every economy and year it gives (1961–2024), as last updated by the World Bank on 2026-11-11; licence, as the series’ own metadata gives it at each build: CC BY-4.0. Its definition, in the World Bank’s words: “Population density is midyear population divided by land area in square kilometers. Population is based on the de facto definition of population, which counts all residents regardless of legal status or citizenship--except for refugees not permanently settled in the country of asylum, who are generally considered part of the population of their country of origin. Land area is a country's total area, excluding area under inland water bodies, national claims to continental shelf, and exclusive economic zones. In most cases the definition of inland water bodies includes major rivers and lakes.” Its sources, as it names them: FAO population estimates, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), publisher: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO); World Bank population estimates, World Bank (WB), publisher: World Bank (WB). Its originators, as the World Bank’s metadata names them, and their own terms: World Bank, whose terms (https://datacatalog.worldbank.org/public-licenses, read 18 November 2026) allow it; Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), whose terms (https://www.fao.org/contact-us/terms/db-terms-of-use/en/, read 20 November 2026) allow it. VM draws each economy’s value on Natural Earth’s countries of today (v5.1.1, 2022), joined by ISO 3166 alpha-3 code, so a value of 1961 is drawn on today’s borders, not on those of 1961; a small state the 1:110 million map leaves out is a point. One of its inputs is FAO’s land area (the series’ own sources name FAO). FAO’s terms for its statistical databases (https://www.fao.org/contact-us/terms/db-terms-of-use/en/, read 20 November 2026) license its datasets under CC BY 4.0 “unless specified otherwise in their metadata or webpage”, allow them to be adapted and re-disseminated, and add that they are not to be used to promote a commercial enterprise or to suggest that FAO endorses one; VM uses them for neither. The land-use domain’s own metadata could not be read: FAOSTAT’s interface asks for authorisation, which VM does not have. VM treats every series resting on FAO’s land area alike, on FAO’s own terms. The 44 aggregates the World Bank also gives (regions, income groups, the world) are not drawn, and are listed under the map’s key. The economies Channel Islands and Gibraltar have a value but no shape or point on Natural Earth’s countries, so VM cannot place them on a free border; the key lists them. The classes are VM’s choice (10, 25, 50, 100, 200 and 500 people per km²), the same for every year. A year with no value for an economy leaves it blank (omni/scripts/build-wb.mjs).

time.shows: the epoch at or before the frame

layers.space: cells of 0.25°, about 28 km across at the equator
layers.status: modelled
layers.legend: Population: GHSL GHS-POP R2023A (European Commission, JRC, Schiavina et al. 2023), CC BY 4.0 – summed into 0.25° cells by Vitruvian Manager
layers.method: VM’s own text. People per km², from GHSL’s GHS-POP R2023A (Schiavina, Freire, Carioli and MacManus 2023, European Commission, Joint Research Centre, doi:10.2905/2FF68A52-5B5B-4A22-8F40-C41DA8332CFE), described in the GHSL Data Package 2023 (doi:10.2760/098587). Licence: CC BY 4.0, which the data’s copyright notice says covers any copyright and sui generis (database) right. What GHSL says of the grids, from its Data Package: the people of each census unit (CIESIN’s GPWv4.11) are spread over the 30 arc-second cells by built-up volume, and the totals are those of the UN’s World Population Prospects 2022 and World Urbanization Prospects 2018; 1975–2020 are modelled from censuses and the built-up surface seen from space, and 2025 and 2030 are projections (“Future grids projections”), which the legend says. How VM made this layer (omni/scripts/build-density.mjs): it added the people of every 30 arc-second cell into cells of 0.25° (about 28 km at the equator) by the cell’s centre, checked each year’s world total against the Data Package’s table 20 (within one part in a million), rounded each 0.25° cell to whole people and left out a cell of fewer than half a person, so the empty sea and ice are blank. Density is the cell’s people over its area on a sphere of radius 6,371.0088 km. The classes are VM’s: the nine deciles of density among the populated cells of 2020, rounded to two significant figures (0.02, 0.12, 0.48, 1.5, 4, 9.9, 23, 54, 150 people per km²), kept the same for every year so a colour means the same density in each. A frame between two epochs shows the epoch before it, and says so; a frame before 1975 shows nothing, and says that GHSL holds 1975 to 2030 (the layer “Population density before 1975 (HYDE)” holds the years before, from HYDE 3.2.1, on the same cells and classes). A cell is a modelled spread of a census, not a count of the people in it: GHSL’s own accuracy notes are in its Data Package.

layers.legend: Population: HYDE 3.2.1 baseline (Klein Goldewijk et al. 2017, Utrecht University and PBL), CC0 1.0 (its readme: CC BY 3.0) – a modelled reconstruction, summed into 0.25° cells by Vitruvian Manager
layers.method: VM’s own text. People per km², from HYDE 3.2.1, the History Database of the Global Environment (Klein Goldewijk, Beusen, Doelman and Stehfest 2017, Utrecht University and PBL Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency), baseline estimate, as the DANS Data Station publishes it (doi:10.17026/DANS-25G-GEZ3). Licence: the repository’s record gives CC0 1.0 (read 20 November 2026), which also waives the EU database right; HYDE’s own readme gives CC BY 3.0, which allows commercial use but says nothing of that right; VM credits HYDE as the readme asks. HYDE’s readme describes it as historical population estimates combined with land use, from 10,000 BCE to 2015 CE, on cells of 5 arc minutes. VM’s note: a cell is a modelled reconstruction, not a count, and the further back the epoch the less it rests on records. How VM made this layer (omni/scripts/build-density-hyde.mjs): it took HYDE’s population counts (popc) for 48 epochs from 4000 BC (the last before the map’s first year, 3400 BC) to AD 1970 (the last before the GHSL grid begins in 1975), added the people of every 5 arc-minute cell into cells of 0.25° (about 28 km at the equator) by the cell’s centre, checked each epoch’s world total against HYDE’s own world total (its table popc_c.txt, within one part in a thousand), rounded each cell to whole people and left out a cell of fewer than half a person. Density is the cell’s people over its area on a sphere of radius 6,371.0088 km. HYDE’s epochs are a thousand years apart before AD 1, a century apart to 1700 and ten years apart after; a frame between two epochs shows the epoch before it, and the legend says which. HYDE’s epoch “0 AD” is left out, since VM counts no year 0 and HYDE does not say whether it means 1 BC or AD 1. The classes are the GHSL grid’s (the nine deciles of density among the populated cells of 2020: 0.02, 0.12, 0.48, 1.5, 4, 9.9, 23, 54, 150 people per km²), so a colour means the same density on both layers. The grid is drawn only as cells, never on today’s countries.

layers.legend: Conflict on territory: UCDP/PRIO Armed Conflict Dataset 26.1 and UCDP Battle-Related Deaths Dataset 26.1 (CC BY 4.0), on Cliopatria v0.2.1 (CC BY 4.0) or Natural Earth (public domain) – processed by Vitruvian Manager
layers.method: VM’s own text. A state is filled in a year when UCDP/PRIO’s Armed Conflict Dataset 26.1 records an armed conflict on its territory that year: a contested incompatibility over government or territory, between two parties of which at least one is a state’s government, with at least 25 battle-related deaths in the year (UCDP’s threshold). The stronger colour is a war, 1,000 or more deaths in the year. From 1989 each conflict’s battle-related deaths are UCDP’s Battle-Related Deaths Dataset 26.1 (conflict level), its best estimate with its low and high; before 1989 VM gives none, because the only series, PRIO’s Battle Deaths Dataset, states no licence. A state that fought outside its own territory that year (a government on either side, primary or secondary, that is not a location of the conflict) is outlined. UCDP names each state by today’s name with the older one in brackets (“Vietnam (North Vietnam)”); VM joins the names to Wikidata Q-ids and ISO3 codes through its own crosswalk, checked on Wikidata at each build, never by a Gleditsch and Ward number. Each state is drawn on Cliopatria’s border for the year, where VM’s crosswalk of Cliopatria holds it, else on Natural Earth’s border of today from the year Wikidata gives as the state’s inception; a state neither holds is listed beside the map, never drawn on a guessed shape. Before 1946 the layer is empty: the Correlates of War, which covers 1926–1945, bars commercial use. 2026 is not in this layer: UCDP’s Candidate Events, which cover it, give counts of events by country and month, not the conflicts and their intensity this layer draws; the layer “Organised violence, UCDP events” shows 2026 from them, marked candidate.
layers.gw: link only: the Retrospective Battlefield’s address names a country by UCDP’s Gleditsch and Ward number (c=), so each state keeps the number UCDP gives it, for that link alone

layers.legend: Elections and referendums: Wikidata (CC0), through the Master Index – placed by Vitruvian Manager
layers.method: VM’s own text. Every election and referendum the Master Index holds with a date and a country (3026 of them), each the Wikidata item’s point in time (P585) at the precision Wikidata records: a date known only to its year is shown as the year, never as 1 January, and one known to its month as the month; where the Master Index stores the precision itself, that is the one kept (one record is known only to the decade or coarser, and placed at its first year). Those still to come on 2026-11-20, the day VM built the layer (28 of them), are drawn hollow and marked expected: their date is the one set, not a record. 4 records are left out as doubtful, because the date Wikidata gives (as the Master Index holds it) is more than a year from the year the item’s own name begins with, and VM does not choose between them: 1911 Croatian parliamentary election (Q15984054), dated 2015-12-17; October 2013 Australian Labor Party leadership election (Q16949505), dated 2010-10-13; 1935 Salvadoran presidential election (Q17087354), dated 1939-01-15; 2026 Slovak referendum (Q139761779), dated 0202-07-04. Each is placed at its country (Wikidata’s country, P17, or the Master Index’s), at the label point of Cliopatria’s polity for the year where VM’s crosswalk of Cliopatria holds the country, else of Natural Earth’s country of today, from 1886 only; one neither holds is listed beside the map, never placed at a guess. The Political Atlas’s election dates are not used: they are written by a language model, not taken from a source a page can name. The Political Retrospective’s are not used either; they are Wikidata’s too, through it.

layers.status: as Wikidata records them
layers.legend: Political change: Wikidata (CC0), each term of the offices of head of state and of government – processed by Vitruvian Manager
layers.method: VM’s own text. For each of today’s sovereign states (Wikidata’s Q3624078), the office it names as its head of state’s (P1906) and its head of government’s (P1313), and every term of those offices Wikidata records (position held, P39, with its start, P580, at Wikidata’s precision; its end, P582, and end cause, P1534, where given). A state is filled in a year when a term begins that year whose holder is not the one before; 7295 terms from 1900, the changes counted from 1926. Wikidata gives an end cause for few terms, so how a leader came and went (by election, coup or death) is shown only where it does, and otherwise said not to be recorded. What this layer cannot give: Archigos’s coding of how each leader entered and left office (regular, irregular, imposed from abroad) and its choice of the effective leader, since Archigos states no licence; the states of the past that are not states today (the Soviet Union, Yugoslavia) are not in this first build. The leaders named are public office-holders only. VM has not checked the terms one by one: Wikidata’s records hold mistakes (a term given to the wrong office, a holder of an office abroad), and each term carries its Wikidata statement so a reader can check it there.

layers.method: VM’s own text. UCDP’s Georeferenced Event Dataset (GED) 26.1, every event from 1989-01 to 2025-12: an event is a day of organised violence with at least one death, state-based (a government against another or against a rebel group), non-state (groups with no government) or one-sided (against civilians). VM counts the events and sums UCDP’s best, low and high deaths in 0.5° cells by month and type, from the month each event began; no actor, side or person is named. UCDP says how exactly it knows each place (where_prec): VM puts the events known to the place, within 25 km, or to a district into cells (1 to 3); those known only to a province or a wider area (4 and 5) are counted by country and month and drawn at the country, not in a cell; those known only to the country, or at sea or in the air (6 and 7), are listed beside the map and never drawn. Countries are joined by ISO3 through VM’s crosswalk of UCDP’s names, never by a Gleditsch and Ward number. A state-based event’s conflict is joined to VM’s war registry, so the map can show one war (l=ucdp-events:w=<id>): each row counts one war’s events, so a war’s total is its own, and a War Focus war holds only its own years. 2026 is UCDP’s Candidate Events (26.01.26.09), as the Realtime Battlefield holds them: by country and month only, and candidate, not yet checked by UCDP; each country is joined by its name through VM’s crosswalk, never by the Realtime file’s Gleditsch and Ward code. A candidate year stays until UCDP’s yearly release records it. The map shows the frame’s year, every month of it, one file loaded at a time (omni/scripts/build-ucdp-events.mjs).
